newsitem.title: UK: UK pensions seen losing 70 bln stg from budget.
newsitem.headline: UK pensions seen losing 70 bln stg from budget.

text.p: British pension plans will see the value of their holdings slashed by changes announced in Wednesday's budget and many companies will have to divert funds to make up shortfalls, industry experts said Thursday.
"From an actuarial point of view Brown has wiped 70 billion stg off the assets of British pension funds," said Andrew Wilson, partner at consultants Watson Wyatt.

British occupational pension funds that had been 100 percent funded will now find themselves with only 86 percent of the money needed to meet their obligations, according to actuaries Sedgewick Noble Lowndes.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's Wednesday budget did away with the credit on Advanced Corporation Tax (ACT) enjoyed by pension funds.
This means that pension funds will see their income reduced, as they are obliged to pay tax on 20 percent of dividends from UK shares that had formerly been sheltered.
Pension fund trustees will now have to revalue downward their holdings in British equities -- estimated at about 60 percent of the 560 billion stg in pension fund assets.

Peter Murray, chairman of the National Association of Pension Funds (NAPF), says that this will force bigger contributions from corporations and cause pension funds to reallocate funds away from UK equities.
"UK equities are now a less attractive asset class. Probably the main beneficiaries will be overseas equities," he told Reuters Financial Television Thursday.
Many British pension funds currently enjoy surpluses and many companies have been able to take contribution holidays.
In the past decade, pension fund contributions of British companies as a percent of operating profits has dipped to less than six percent from around nine percent in 1986, according to BZW research.

"Pension schemes generally are in a good financial state but there is a significant minority that has no surplus and another group that has probably seen its surplus wiped out by this change," said Ross Russell, of the Association of British Actuaries.
This could have a major effect on some of the largest British listed companies, according to analyst Richard Kersley of BZW.
In a recent research note Kersley said that the abolition of the ACT credit will disproportionately hit companies which have large pension funds in proportion to market value.
Kersley cited British Steel, Rolls Royce, British Telecom and British Aerospace as among those that could be hardest hit by falls in the value of pension fund assets.
"Over the medium term we will see contributions to pension schemes going up," said Russell.
He estimates that of the top 100 British companies about 95 of them have defined benefit schemes. Under defined benefit schemes the onus for making up any shortfall falls on the company.
The abolition of the ACT credit may also put British pension funds in danger of running afoul of new pensions legislation introduced in April, according to Gordon Bagot, of consultants WM Company.
A recent survey of member by the NAPF found that about half said they will have to take immediate action to top up pension funds, the organisation said.
